analysis.one_liner: Bans employers from forcing workers to sign away their right to sue or join class actions over work disputes.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate labor committee on the day it was introduced in June 2024 and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Most large employers require workers to sign arbitration agreements as a condition of hire, which means disputes over pay, discrimination, or firing go to a private arbitrator instead of a court, and workers usually cannot band together in class actions. This bill would make those pre-dispute agreements unenforceable for work disputes, let workers choose arbitration only voluntarily after a dispute arises, and ban retaliation against anyone who refuses. It would also amend labor law to protect workers' right to pursue claims jointly or as a class.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers — including independent contractors regardless of how they are labeled — who would regain access to courts and to class or collective actions for wage, discrimination, and other work-related claims. The bill covers domestic workers and applies to disputes arising after enactment, even under older agreements [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers locked out of court by arbitration clauses

how_it_helps.text: Pre-dispute arbitration agreements requiring arbitration of work disputes would be invalid and unenforceable, and pre-dispute waivers of joint, class, or collective claims would be banned outright [S2].

After a dispute arises, a worker could still agree to arbitrate, but only voluntarily: no coercion, plain-language written notice of the right to refuse, a 45-day waiting period with the clock on legal deadlines paused, and written affirmative consent [S2].
Employers could not retaliate against or threaten a worker for refusing to arbitrate, and workers injured by such retaliation could sue with attorney's fees available [S2].

The bill would add a prohibited practice to the National Labor Relations Act covering agreements that force employees to give up the right to pursue joint, class, or collective claims, overriding the Supreme Court's Epic Systems decision, which the bill's findings say allows employers to impose such waivers as a condition of employment [S2].
The protections would cover not just employees but independent contractors regardless of classification, and explicitly include domestic service workers in households [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that rely on mandatory arbitration and class-action waivers — large companies in particular — would face more workplace claims in court, including class actions, along with litigation costs and jury exposure. The private arbitration industry would lose a large volume of employer-driven caseload.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers using forced arbitration, and arbitration providers

drawbacks.text: Businesses argue that resolving disputes one-on-one in arbitration is faster and cheaper than court litigation for many workers, and that class actions channel most of their value to attorneys' fees while exposing employers to costly litigation that can affect wages and hiring; the bill text itself notes arbitration was originally designed for commercial parties of similar bargaining power, but supporters of arbitration point to its speed and lower cost [S2].

Courts and employers would absorb substantially more individual employment lawsuits once mandatory arbitration ends, and the bill allows claims to proceed in court for disputes arising after enactment even under agreements signed years earlier [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is access versus efficiency. Workers under mandatory arbitration clauses currently have little practical choice — they often do not realize they have waived court access, and joining a class action is frequently the only affordable way to pursue a claim [S2]. Removing that constraint restores leverage to individual workers, at the cost of more litigation for employers and the courts. The bill limits the change by leaving voluntary post-dispute arbitration available and carving out collective bargaining agreements.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which took no action on it before the 118th Congress ended, so it died in committee.

narrative.text: Sen. Patty Murray introduced the bill on June 11, 2024, joined by 18 original cosponsors including Sens. Sanders, Warren, Durbin, and Blumenthal [S1].
The Senate read it twice and referred it the same day to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, its only committee assignment [S4].
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — appears in the action history before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that rely on mandatory arbitration clauses keep the status quo: workers' claims stay in private arbitration without class actions, and nothing changed for arbitration providers either.

for.name: Patty Murray
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban forced arbitration in work disputes and recruited 18 original cosponsors.

for.name: Original cosponsors (18 senators)
for.role: Sen. Murray, Blumenthal, Sanders, Durbin, Merkley, Warren, Padilla, Klobuchar, Booker, Casey, Hirono, Cortez Masto, Baldwin, Brown, Murphy, Markey, Reed, and Shaheen
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction; total support reached 19 senators, all Democrats or independents.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 cosponsors were Democrats or independents, with no Republican support recorded, and the bill never advanced beyond its Democratic-led committee referral [S3].

industries.note: These employers currently resolve wage, discrimination, and firing disputes in private arbitration without class actions; the bill would return those disputes to public courts and allow workers to sue together. Their cost of defending claims would rise, while workers' ability to recover would grow [S2].

industries.industry: Private arbitration providers (e.g., commercial arbitration firms)
industries.note: Much of the arbitration industry's employment caseload exists because employers require arbitration at hire; banning pre-dispute arbitration agreements for work disputes would shrink that business [S2].

The bill exempts arbitration provisions in union contracts from its ban but bars them from waiving a worker's right to judicially enforce statutory rights — union-negotiated arbitration survives with limits [S2].
